beats.text: In 2019, Facebook was fined five billion dollars. [BEAT] The largest penalty in FTC history.
beats.why: A news anchor announcing the exact $5B fine gives the cold open instant credibility — this is archival proof of the fact being stated, not generic footage. The broadcast chyron 'Facebook $5B Fine' is on-screen text reinforcing the hook stat.

beats.text: [BEAT] Eighty-seven million people's data — harvested, profiled, and sold to a political targeting firm without their knowledge.
beats.why: The narration names the data harvesting and political targeting firm — Cambridge Analytica is the subject. This clip shows the scandal being reported in real time, visually grounding the 87M figure in the actual event rather than abstract stock imagery.

beats.text: [BEAT] And on the day the fine was announced, [PAUSE:1.0] Facebook's stock went up.
beats.why: The narration's central irony — the fine day, stock went UP — requires a chart with annotation proving it. This is the exact visual evidence: an annotated Facebook stock chart showing the price movement on the day of the FTC settlement. No clip can match this specificity.
beats.sfx_motivation: The inverted-outcome revelation is the thesis of the entire documentary — a hard impact hit forces the viewer's brain to stop and process the contradiction before the narration continues.

beats.text: The market added six billion dollars in value.
beats.why: The narration says 'the market added six billion dollars' — cutting to live NYSE trading floor footage connects the abstract $6B number to the physical place where that money moved. Ted Weisberg and the trading floor crowd make this concrete and real.

beats.text: Mark Zuckerberg personally gained one point one billion dollars in a single day.
beats.why: Zuckerberg is named for the first time — this is his character introduction. The Senate hearing footage shows him walking through a press scrum, projecting both power and culpability simultaneously, which is exactly the tension the narration ($1.1B personal gain) requires.

beats.text: [BEAT] The punishment made the company richer than if the government had done nothing.
beats.why: The FTC official declaring the fine was a 'watershed moment' while the narration reveals it made Facebook richer creates documentary irony. The government's own press conference footage — meant to project consequence — now proves the opposite of what it intended.
beats.clip_audio_quote: Facebook betrayed the trust of its users and deceived them about their ability to control their personal information

beats.text: How is that possible?
beats.why: The rhetorical question 'How is that possible?' demands a visual that holds the contradiction on screen. A data chart showing Zuckerberg's personal gain versus the fine amount lets the viewer sit with the math — the image IS the answer to the question.
beats.sfx_motivation: The whoosh punctuates the rhetorical question and signals a hard pivot in time — clearing the palate before the 1977 setup begins.

beats.text: To understand, you need to go back to 1977. Because someone had to discover this trick.
beats.why: The narration pivots to 1977 and introduces the Ford Pinto as the origin of the trick. A clean static shot of the Pinto car — before the fire — establishes the object at the center of the story and builds suspense before the explosion footage hits on the next beat.

beats.text: [BEAT] And the discovery started with a car on fire.
beats.why: The narration says 'a car on fire' — this is the actual 1977 crash test footage of the Pinto exploding. It is the most direct possible illustration of the words being spoken and delivers the visceral payoff promised by 'car on fire.' Nothing substitutes for the real thing.

beats.text: In 1977, Ford knew the Pinto's fuel tank ruptured in rear-end collisions. They had the crash test data.
beats.why: The narration specifies 'crash test data' — Ford knew. A freeze-frame still from the actual crash test at the moment of rear-impact shows the evidence Ford possessed internally. The still (versus the motion clip) signals a shift from emotional impact to cold analytical facts: Ford saw this and chose profit.

beats.text: [CHAPTER: THE FORMULA]
beats.why: Chapter card marks new section

beats.text: Two engineers wrote a cost-benefit analysis — an actual document, with actual numbers.
beats.why: Narration references 'an actual document, with actual numbers' — this image IS that document. Showing the cost-benefit memo while describing it grounds the abstraction in physical reality and makes the corporate calculation feel obscene rather than theoretical.

beats.text: [BEAT] Fix every Pinto: one hundred and thirty-seven million dollars. Expected wrongful death payouts: forty-nine point five million.
beats.why: The narration reads the two numbers aloud — $137M to fix vs $49.5M in deaths. The data visualization makes the comparison visceral and scannable. Viewers see the math that killed people, not just hear it. This is the thesis of the entire documentary in one image.
beats.text_overlay: $137M to fix. $49.5M to pay for deaths.

beats.text: [PAUSE:1.5] They shipped the car.
beats.why: Three words: 'They shipped the car.' The freeze-frame of the Pinto crash test — the car mid-impact, fire beginning — is the punch. Showing the consequence of the spreadsheet decision exactly as the narrator delivers the verdict. Hold this image in silence for the full PAUSE.
beats.sfx_motivation: Hard impact sound on 'They shipped the car' — the moment the abstraction becomes flesh. First of two chapter SFX.

beats.text: A thirteen-year-old boy named Richard Grimshaw was a passenger in a Pinto that was rear-ended in San Bernardino.
beats.why: The narration introduces Richard Grimshaw — a specific child in a specific car in a specific place. Rolling footage of the Pinto rear-impact crash test makes the abstraction real: this is the car, this is what happens when a car is rear-ended. Muted — narration carries the emotional weight here.

beats.text: The fuel tank ruptured. [BEAT] The driver burned to death. Richard survived — barely. [BEAT] Burned over his entire body.
beats.why: The narration describes the fuel tank rupturing and a driver burning to death. This still captures the Pinto fully engulfed — flames visible, car destroyed. The freeze-frame forces the viewer to sit with the image while hearing 'burned to death.' Motion would feel exploitative; a held still feels like a reckoning.

beats.text: Lost parts of his fingers. Lost his left ear. Years of skin grafts. [BEAT] A childhood replaced by hospital rooms.
beats.why: Narration catalogs Richard's injuries — fingers, ear, skin grafts, hospital rooms. A different angle of the same fire crash aftermath shifts the visual perspective from the spectacle of the explosion to its aftermath, mirroring the narration's shift from the event to its human cost. Slow zoom into the wreckage.

beats.text: The jury awarded one hundred and twenty-five million dollars in punitive damages — the largest in American history.
beats.why: The jury verdict — $125M, largest punitive damages in US history — is a justice system response. The gavel is the right visual because it represents the moment accountability is supposed to happen. The text overlay delivers the number while the image signals 'the system responded.' Sets up the betrayal in beat 7.
beats.text_overlay: $125,000,000 — largest punitive damages in US history

beats.text: The judge reduced it to three point five million. Ford was acquitted of criminal homicide.
beats.why: The judge reduces $125M to $3.5M and Ford is acquitted of criminal homicide. Cutting to the DOJ building facade — the physical embodiment of federal justice — creates ironic visual contrast. The building stands for accountability; the narration reveals accountability failed. The architecture indicts itself.

beats.text: [BEAT] No executive went to prison. The fine was three point five million dollars. Ford kept selling cars.
beats.why: No executive went to prison. Ford kept selling cars. The image of the Pinto on the road — not burning, just driving, ordinary — is the horror. After five beats of crash footage and grief, seeing the car just... exist... makes the impunity concrete. This is what 'kept selling cars' looks like.
beats.text_overlay: No prison. No recall. Ford kept selling.

beats.text: No one went to prison. [BEAT] And somewhere in a boardroom, someone noticed something.
beats.why: The final line — 'And somewhere in a boardroom, someone noticed something' — is the hinge of the entire documentary. The empty boardroom table is the right visual because it's ominous without being explicit. Someone was here. They saw what Ford did. They drew a conclusion. The empty room implies what comes next without showing it. Slow zoom into the head of the table.
beats.sfx_motivation: Low tension riser building under 'someone noticed something' — this is the turning point where the documentary shifts from case study to systemic thesis. Second of two chapter SFX.

beats.text: [PAUSE:1.5] The cost of getting caught was less than the cost of doing the right thing.
beats.why: The narration crystallizes the Ford Pinto thesis — 'cost of getting caught < cost of doing right.' This is the actual cost-benefit analysis document Ford wrote, making the abstract argument literal. The document IS the formula.

beats.text: That might have been an isolated scandal. A single bad company making a single bad calculation. [PAUSE:1.0] Except it wasn't.
beats.why: The narration pivots from Ford's 'isolated' scandal to the systemic pattern. A multi-company fine comparison chart visually proves the word 'isolated' is false before the narration even finishes saying 'Except it wasn't.'

beats.text: In 2010, a twenty-four-year-old bank teller named Yesenia Guitron did something dangerous. [BEAT] She told the truth.
beats.why: Yesenia Guitron is being introduced as a Wells Fargo bank teller who witnessed the fraud firsthand. The a-roll opens on Wells Fargo's scandal coverage — 'a bank teller did something dangerous' lands harder over real news footage of the institution she worked for. The [BEAT] pause before 'She told the truth' is the cut point.
beats.clip_audio_quote: for years, Wells Fargo employees created millions of unauthorized accounts on behalf of their customers
beats.sfx_motivation: The [BEAT] marker before 'She told the truth' is a genuine dramatic beat — the moment a low-level employee's courage is framed as the dangerous act.

beats.text: She'd watched her colleagues at Wells Fargo open accounts that customers never asked for — credit cards ordered to addresses that didn't exist, savings accounts funded by moving money between other accounts without permission.
beats.why: Narration describes 'credit cards ordered to addresses that didn't exist.' This still is an extreme close-up of an embossed silver credit card — exactly the physical object being described. Specific > generic.

beats.text: She knew why they did it. There was a quota: every customer should have eight products.
beats.why: The Wells Fargo branch storefront grounds the quota system in the physical institution that enforced it. 'Eight products per customer' — this is where that pressure originated. The bank facade is the face of the system.

beats.text: "Eight is Great." [BEAT] Miss the number and you get a warning. Miss it again and you get fired.
beats.why: A close-up hand writing on paper — visually matches the act of opening fraudulent accounts, signing paperwork that shouldn't exist. 'Miss it again and you get fired' — the pen is the instrument of coercion.

beats.text: So the tellers cheated. Because the alternative was unemployment. Yesenia called the company's ethics hotline and reported the fraud.
beats.why: Yesenia calls the ethics hotline — this is her whistleblower moment. The corporate_whistleblower a-roll footage establishes the institutional context around what whistleblowing actually means and costs. Muted so narration stays primary; the visual category (whistleblower coverage) does the semantic work.

beats.text: [BEAT] Wells Fargo terminated her the same week. She never found steady work in banking again.
beats.why: Wells Fargo branch exterior — but now it reads as the institution that just destroyed someone's career. 'Terminated her the same week' needs the bank itself on screen, not a person, because the institution is the perpetrator. The [BEAT] before this line demands a hard, cold cut.

beats.text: Her name went on an industry blacklist — a record that follows you like a scar.
beats.why: The industry blacklist is the systemic retaliation mechanism — not a Wells Fargo action but an industry-wide one. Shifting to a generic whistleblower image signals the camera zooming out from Yesenia's story to the structural pattern, matching the narration's move from personal to systemic.

beats.text: Three point five million fake accounts. Five thousand three hundred tellers fired for opening them.
beats.why: The punchline stats — 3.5M fake accounts, 5,300 tellers fired — demand a data visual that makes the scale undeniable. This is the specific Wells Fargo accounts chart. The numbers need to be ON SCREEN while the narrator says them, not just spoken into abstraction.
beats.sfx_motivation: The scale of the fraud — 3.5 million accounts — is a genuine stat revelation that earns a highlight SFX. This is the second and final SFX for this chapter.

beats.text: And the woman who designed the quota — Carrie Tolstedt, head of Community Banking — kept fifty-seven million dollars and got zero prison time.
beats.why: Wells Fargo scandal testimony footage grounds the Tolstedt reveal — the a-roll framing of a documented scandal makes '$57M kept, zero prison time' land as institutional fact rather than editorial claim

beats.text: She served her sentence at home. [BEAT] Ford's formula required a memo.
beats.why: An ordinary customer at a Wells Fargo ATM contrasts silently with an executive serving her sentence at home — the visual indicts the asymmetry of consequence without a word spoken

beats.text: Wells Fargo's didn't even require a decision — just a number and a threat.
beats.why: The fake-accounts data chart makes 'just a number and a threat' concrete — the audience sees the quota system's output as arithmetic, not abstraction, at the exact moment narration names it

beats.text: Ford needed a document to do this. Wells Fargo only needed a quota. [PAUSE:1.5] The next company didn't need either.
beats.why: A hand signing a blank sheet literalizes 'Ford needed a document / Wells Fargo only needed a quota' — the empty page is the quota itself, the most banal instrument of mass fraud, held in frame through the pause before the pivot to Purdue

beats.text: It just needed a head start.
beats.why: First appearance of Purdue Pharma branding — 'It just needed a head start' lands harder when the viewer immediately reads the company name; the image plants the reveal before the narration explains what the head start was

beats.text: Purdue Pharma saw the lawsuits coming a decade early and withdrew ten point seven billion dollars from the company before anyone could calculate the fine.
beats.why: Purdue Pharma / Sackler family court or press photograph pairs with the $10.7B withdrawal stat — puts a face to the asset strip and makes the preemptive money-move feel deliberate, not accidental

beats.text: [BEAT] Richard Sackler promised a, quote, blizzard of prescriptions at OxyContin's launch.
beats.why: Richard Sackler's face must be on screen when his name and his own words are spoken — 'blizzard of prescriptions' requires a human being attached to it; without the face, it remains a corporate abstraction instead of a personal decision

beats.text: In Kermit, West Virginia — population four hundred — a single pharmacy received nine million opioid pills in two years.
beats.why: Opioid crisis imagery (pill bottles, the epidemic's visual shorthand) grounds the Kermit, WV stat — 9 million pills to a town of 400 is numerically incomprehensible; the familiar opioid-bottle image translates the abstraction into something the viewer already has an emotional relationship with

beats.text: [BEAT] The pharmacist went to prison. The Sacklers moved their money. [BEAT] More than eight hundred thousand Americans died.
beats.why: The clip's on-camera news testimony about the Sackler family and the epidemic delivers the visual weight of a third-party witness at the exact moment narration lands '800,000 dead' — muted so the number is heard cleanly, but the presence of a real broadcaster speaking into camera amplifies the credibility of the death toll
beats.sfx_motivation: 800,000 deaths is the largest human cost of any case study in the video — a single hard impact sting punctuates the sentence and signals this is the emotional peak of the chapter

beats.text: The settlement: seven point four billion. The family's remaining fortune: thirteen billion. [PAUSE:1.5] Nine thousand dollars per death.
beats.why: The deaths-vs-settlement data chart makes '$9,000 per death' a visual equation, not just a spoken number — the chart closes the chapter with the arithmetic of impunity laid out on screen so the viewer can sit with it through the 1.5s pause that follows
beats.sfx_motivation: 'Nine thousand dollars per death' is the thesis-in-miniature for the entire video — a highlight sting punctuates the pause and seals the chapter

beats.text: Ford valued a life at two hundred thousand in 1977. The Sacklers got it down to nine thousand.
beats.why: The narration invokes the Ford Pinto cost-benefit memo directly — $200K per life. This image shows the actual document math that valued human lives at a dollar figure, grounding the abstract claim in the artifact the audience already associates with Ford's calculus. The contrast with $9,000 (Sackler) lands harder when the $200,000 number has a paper trail on screen.

beats.text: The fine is cheaper than the profit. Every time. [BEAT] Without exception.
beats.why: The narration delivers the central economic thesis: the fine is always cheaper than the profit. A comparison chart directly visualizes this ratio across companies. Matching the data visualization to the spoken claim at the exact moment it lands gives the viewer something concrete — the visual proves what the words assert rather than merely illustrating them.

beats.text: The law doesn't prevent corporate crime. [BEAT] It prices it.
beats.why: The thesis line of the entire video — 'The law doesn't prevent corporate crime. It prices it.' — lands against the facade of the institution whose entire purpose is preventing corporate crime. The DOJ building is the punchline. The visual irony is the argument: the building that should be the solution is, on screen, the evidence.
beats.sfx_motivation: The single most important line in the video. Maximum dramatic punctuation lands on the word 'prices' — the reframe that recontextualizes every case study the audience just watched.

beats.text: And the price keeps dropping.
beats.why: 'The price keeps dropping' is a trend statement. This chart shows the fine-settle cycle across repeat offenders, giving the viewer the downward shape of the argument before the aggregate statistics land in the next two beats. Seeing the pattern visually primes the audience for the numbers that follow.

beats.text: Since 2000, corporations have paid over one trillion dollars in fines and settlements in the United States alone.
beats.why: The narration delivers the macro statistic: $1 trillion in fines since 2000. This chart exists to visualize exactly that number. Matching the data graphic to the spoken stat at the moment it is said is the most direct evidence beat possible — the visual is the source, not a metaphor for it.

beats.text: One hundred and twenty-seven companies have each paid more than a billion.
beats.why: 127 companies paying $1B+ each represents the financial establishment itself. The overhead NYSE trading floor shot conveys institutional density and scale — dozens of actors operating within the same system, matching the abstraction of '127 companies' with a visual of exactly that kind of concentrated, systemic activity.

beats.text: [PAUSE:1.5] And here's the number that should end every argument about whether the system works: [BEAT] companies caught repeatedly pay smaller fines as a percentage of their revenue over time.
beats.why: The narration describes the recidivism discount — repeat violators pay smaller fines as a percentage of revenue over time. A settlement check is the literal object being described: the piece of paper that closes the case and lets the company walk. Holding on it during the 12-second beat (with pause) gives the viewer time to absorb what the check represents — not punishment, but a receipt.

beats.text: Not larger. Smaller. [BEAT] The more you violate, the better the deal gets.
beats.why: The WAN Show hosts reacting in real time — 'This is like some next level BS' — mirrors the audience's own response to the recidivism discount. Playing a genuine human reaction under 'the more you violate, the better the deal gets' lets the viewer's outrage be reflected back before the narration provides the intellectual frame. The reaction validates the emotion the audience is already feeling.
beats.clip_audio_quote: This is like some next level BS. This explains not all, but at least some of how
beats.sfx_motivation: Second SFX of the chapter — the systemic reveal that recidivism is structurally rewarded is a genuine shock that earns a dramatic audio punctuation before the clip reaction lands.

beats.text: Each company added one feature to the original calculation. Ford added a memo. Wells Fargo added plausible deniability.
beats.why: The narration names Wells Fargo specifically — 'Wells Fargo added plausible deniability.' This still of the Wells Fargo branch exterior grounds the named institution at the exact moment it appears in the narration. Ford was handled in beat 0 with its document; Wells Fargo gets its building. The parallel structure reinforces that these are not accidents but a pattern.

beats.text: Purdue added preemption. Facebook added scale.
beats.why: The narration names Purdue first in the final enumeration. The Purdue b-roll news footage — 'eight members of the Sackler family caused much of the opioid epidemic' — gives the 'preemption' abstraction a face and a scale. At 2.5 seconds, video motion is more visceral than a static still, and the broadcast framing signals that this was news — something that happened, not just a case study.

beats.text: [BEAT] But every one of them had something in common — the damage, at least in theory, could be reversed.
beats.why: The gavel physically represents the legal system's theoretical corrective power — the very concept the narration is establishing before revealing it collapses. 'Could be reversed' needs a symbol of institutional justice on screen so the viewer understands what's about to be taken away.

beats.text: Ford could recall the car. Wells Fargo could close the accounts. Purdue could stop making the pills.
beats.why: Ford is named first and the recall is the most concrete of the three reversals — a physical car that can be pulled back. The Pinto still (vehicle, not explosion) represents the product existing before accountability, reinforcing 'Ford could recall the car' as the most legible example of the trio.

beats.text: Then the formula met the internet. And the damage became permanent.
beats.why: Rows of servers extending to infinity physically embody 'the formula met the internet' — the infrastructure of permanence. Cutting to this on 'Then' creates the chapter pivot: the old formula (cars, banks, pills) against the new one (data that cannot be recalled, closed, or stopped).
beats.sfx_motivation: 'The damage became permanent' is the thesis break between eras — the hardest statement in the chapter. An impact hit cements the irreversibility before the Facebook section opens.

beats.text: Facebook was the bridge between the old formula and the new one.
beats.why: Facebook's physical headquarters establishes the company as the chapter's central entity the moment it is named. 'Facebook was the bridge' demands the brand appear on screen — an HQ establishing shot signals to the viewer this is who the next ten minutes are about.

beats.text: [CHAPTER: THE DATA]
beats.why: Chapter card marks new section

beats.text: In 2013, a Cambridge University researcher named Aleksandr Kogan built a personality quiz app.
beats.why: Cambridge Analytica imagery directly names the organization Kogan fed data into — the narration introduces the researcher and his quiz app, and the viewer needs the Cambridge Analytica brand identity on screen immediately to anchor who benefits from what follows.

beats.text: Two hundred and seventy thousand people downloaded it.
beats.why: A blurry smartphone screen grounds 270,000 downloads in the tactile reality of a person tapping an app — the innocuous gesture that unknowingly opened a data pipeline to 87 million. The intimacy of the phone shot makes the statistic personal before the scale explodes in beat 8.

beats.text: [BEAT] But Facebook's API — the system that connects apps to the platform — gave the quiz access to not just those users' data, but all of their friends' data too.
beats.why: This A-roll covers the precise API mechanism the narration is describing — the quiz app's access cascading through friends' data. It is the most credible visual anchor for a technical explanation: actual journalism covering the actual exploit, played mute so narration carries the explanation.

beats.text: Every like, every post, every photo, every connection.
beats.why: The Facebook brand identity — its entire visual surface — represents the totality of what was harvested: 'every like, every post, every photo, every connection.' The narration stacks data categories; the platform's own logo is the container that held all of it.

beats.text: [BEAT] Two hundred and seventy thousand downloads became eighty-seven million people's data harvested in weeks.
beats.why: A Cambridge Analytica data visualization makes the scale explosion legible — 270K to 87M is not intuitive without a graphic showing the network amplification. This is the chapter's central stat and the most shareable number; it needs to land as a data moment, not just a spoken number.
beats.sfx_motivation: 87 million is the chapter's defining number — the moment the viewer realizes the scale of the exploit. A highlight sound cues the stat landing and rewards attention.

beats.text: Facebook knew this was possible.
beats.why: 'Facebook knew this was possible' is the most damning sentence in the chapter — it converts negligence into intent. Zuckerberg walking into the Senate hearing surrounded by cameras is the definitive image of that knowing: the most powerful tech executive in history entering a room where he must account for it.

beats.text: [BEAT] It was a feature, not a bug — they'd designed the API to be open because open APIs drive engagement, and engagement drives advertising revenue.
beats.why: Narration explains Facebook's deliberate API design philosophy — the company HQ grounds this as a corporate strategy decision, not an accident, matching the 'feature not a bug' framing.

beats.text: In 2014, they quietly changed the rules. But they never enforced deletion of the data already taken.
beats.why: Narration describes the quiet 2014 rule change and the failure to enforce data deletion — this data visualization of Cambridge Analytica's data flows makes the abstract 'data already taken' concrete and visible.

beats.text: Cambridge Analytica used that data to build voter profiles so precise they could predict what would make you angry before you felt it.
beats.why: Direct visual evidence for Cambridge Analytica building voter profiles — this image shows the voter data operation specifically, matching the narration about predicting what would make you angry.

beats.text: [BEAT] They were hired by the Trump campaign. They were hired by groups supporting Brexit.
beats.why: Narration names the Trump campaign and Brexit — the US Capitol building anchors the political scale of this data weaponization, the place where democracy was supposed to protect against exactly this.

beats.text: Eighty-seven million people's personalities — measured, modeled, and weaponized — for the price of a free quiz they never took.
beats.why: The '87 million people' stat is the scale revelation of this chapter — Cambridge Analytica imagery paired with the stat overlay gives the number a face and a source, making the abstraction land as a real event.
beats.sfx_motivation: The number 87 million is the gut-punch of this section — a single hard impact hit underscores the scale at the moment the stat lands.

beats.text: [BEAT] And most of them still don't know.
beats.why: Two-second beat — 'And most of them still don't know.' Holding on Cambridge Analytica's own identity forces the viewer to sit with the asymmetry: the organization knows everything, the targets know nothing.

beats.text: A 2019 Pew survey found that seventy-four percent of Facebook users didn't know the platform maintained a list of their interests and traits for ad targeting.
beats.why: Narration cites the 2019 Pew survey showing 74% of users didn't know Facebook tracked their interests — Facebook HQ as backdrop makes clear this was the company's deliberate opacity, not user ignorance.

beats.text: They didn't know they'd been profiled. They didn't know their data had been sold.
beats.why: Still shows Zuckerberg in a CNN Breaking News chyron — narration says they didn't know their data was sold. Zuckerberg on a news chyron is the institutional face of what was done to them, the gap between executive knowledge and user ignorance.

beats.text: [BEAT] They just knew that their feed felt different in 2016 — angrier, more anxious, more polarized — and they assumed that was the world changing.
beats.why: Narration describes people noticing their feed felt angrier and more polarized in 2016 — someone scrolling a social media feed on a phone is the viewer's own experience, making the abstract algorithm effect feel personal and recognizable.

beats.text: [PAUSE:1.0] It wasn't the world. It was the algorithm.
beats.why: Final line — 'It wasn't the world. It was the algorithm.' Zuckerberg surrounded by a crush of photographers walking into the Senate hearing is the perfect payoff image: the algorithm has a face, and it's sitting in front of Congress because of exactly this.
beats.sfx_motivation: One-beat pause after 'It was the algorithm' — a low tension sting here lets the revelation breathe before the chapter continues.

beats.text: Tuned by their own data, sold without their consent, deployed to shape an election.
beats.why: Narration says data was 'deployed to shape an election' — Cambridge Analytica voter-targeting document is the exact artifact of that crime. Specific, damning, and immediately legible as political data manipulation. No generic image captures this as precisely.

beats.text: When the story broke in March 2018, Zuckerberg was summoned before Congress. He wore a suit. He said sorry.
beats.why: Narration says 'Zuckerberg was summoned before Congress. He wore a suit.' — the a-roll of Zuckerberg arriving at the Senate hearing is the primary source footage for this exact event. The image of him in a suit navigating press matches the wording beat-for-beat.

beats.text: And then something happened that tells you everything about why the formula survives.
beats.why: Narration teases 'something happened that tells you everything about why the formula survives' — the packed gallery of senators, cameras, and press in the hearing room builds institutional weight and dread before the punchline lands. Wide frame emphasizes the stakes.

beats.text: A United States senator — a person with the power to regulate the most valuable company on Earth — looked at Mark Zuckerberg and asked: "How does Facebook make money if the product is free?"
beats.why: Narration describes 'a senator with the power to regulate the most valuable company on Earth' — the crowded formal hearing room (val=8, 9.6s beat allows hold) shows the full spectacle of power assembled around Zuckerberg. Text overlay delivers the senator's question verbatim while the visual anchors it in reality.
beats.text_overlay: "How does Facebook make money if the product is free?"

beats.text: Zuckerberg paused. [BEAT] And said: "Senator, we run ads."
beats.why: Narration delivers 'Senator, we run ads' — the a-roll of Zuckerberg at the hearing is the source footage for this exact exchange. Face close-up at the moment of the punchline maximizes impact. Text overlay pins the quote onscreen so viewers feel it land. Second and final use of this clip, saved for the chapter's highest-stakes beat.
beats.sfx_motivation: The 'Senator, we run ads' line is the chapter's central revelation — a sitting U.S. senator didn't understand how the most profitable surveillance company on Earth worked. Impact SFX punctuates the moment the punchline lands.

beats.text: The room laughed. The internet turned it into a meme.
beats.why: Narration says 'the room laughed / the internet turned it into a meme' — a distinct still of Zuckerberg at the hearing anchors the physical setting of the laugh before the narration pivots to the internet's reaction. Different file from the .mp4 clip already used twice; maintains visual continuity without repetition.

beats.text: For weeks, the clip circulated as comedy — an old senator, a young CEO, a punchline about boomers not understanding technology.
beats.why: Narration says 'for weeks the clip circulated as comedy' — the CNN Breaking News chyron featuring Zuckerberg (val=8) is the specific visual of media amplification that turned this exchange into a meme. A TV still of him on-air represents 'circulation' far better than another hearing room shot. This is a still, not the 2+-used .mp4.

beats.text: And it was funny. It genuinely was.

beats.text: Let me show you what the math looks like when you put a face on it.
beats.why: Opening with the Pinto wreckage primes the viewer that 'putting a face on the math' means real burned bodies — the abstraction of cost-benefit analysis is about to become a person. The smoldering car is the bridge between formula and flesh.

beats.text: Richard Grimshaw survived the Pinto fire.
beats.why: Grimshaw's name lands on the exact image of the Pinto fire crash that scarred him — the viewer sees the moment that defined the rest of his life. Cut is tight because the beat is only 1.9s; the image must hit on his name.

beats.text: He grew up carrying scars that covered his body and a verdict that was supposed to change things — one hundred and twenty-five million dollars, reduced to three point five million.
beats.why: The dark, grainy low-resolution still holds the weight of 'scars that covered his body' — the degraded image quality mirrors the diminished verdict. Staying on Pinto footage while narrating the $125M→$3.5M reduction keeps causality visible: this car, these scars, this price.

beats.text: [PAUSE:1.0] The message was: we've done the math, and your pain has a price.
beats.why: After the PAUSE, the DOJ entrance — the building that is supposed to protect people — becomes an indictment. 'Your pain has a price' spoken over the house of justice makes the irony physical. The cold stone facade is the math made architecture.
beats.sfx_motivation: Thesis crystallization moment — 'your pain has a price' is the emotional center of the entire video. One low impact on the word 'price'.

beats.text: [BEAT] Ford paid it and moved on. Yesenia Guitron called the ethics hotline and was fired for it.
beats.why: The whistleblower news package directly contextualizes Guitron — she called the ethics hotline and was fired, exactly the pattern the clip covers. The contrast lands harder with real news anchors saying 'traitor' over footage of people who reported fraud.

beats.text: She never worked in banking again. [BEAT] Carrie Tolstedt, who built the quota system, kept fifty-seven million dollars.
beats.why: The Wells Fargo office interior puts the institutional backdrop against both halves of the sentence: Guitron never worked in banking again (forced out of this world), while Tolstedt kept $57M (rewarded by it). The corporate interior is the same building that protected the executive and expelled the whistleblower.

beats.text: The Sackler name is still on a wing of the Guggenheim Museum in New York City.
beats.why: The Guggenheim exterior is the only visual that makes the Sackler-on-the-wall claim concrete and credible. Viewers recognize the Frank Lloyd Wright spiral — it's one of the most famous museums in the world. That familiarity is what makes the name being on the wall feel wrong.

beats.text: The Metropolitan Museum took theirs down after public outcry. [BEAT] The Guggenheim hasn't.
beats.why: Staying on the Guggenheim for both the Met comparison and 'the Guggenheim hasn't' makes the point visually: we are looking at the building that chose to keep the name. A second angle of the same museum reinforces that this is a specific, real, present-tense fact — not history.

beats.text: You can walk into one of the most prestigious cultural institutions in the world, look up at the wall, and read the name of a family that earned their fortune from a drug that killed eight hundred thousand people.
beats.why: The longest beat in the chapter (12s) needs the pivot from institution to human cost. 'Eight hundred thousand people' can't land over a museum facade — it needs faces and bodies. The opioid crisis image supplies the human scale the Guggenheim exterior cannot. The museum pays for cultural legitimacy; this image shows what was purchased with.

beats.text: [BEAT] They kept thirteen billion. And they kept the wall.
beats.why: The chapter's closing line — 'they kept thirteen billion, and they kept the wall' — needs the Purdue corporate identity to close the loop. The Guggenheim beat was about the name on the wall; this beat names the company that put it there. Purdue Pharma imagery as the final image of the chapter makes the accountability failure the last thing the viewer sees before the next chapter.
beats.sfx_motivation: Final beat of the Reckoning chapter — the closing punch of the entire case study sequence. Deep impact on 'the wall' lands the irony of cultural whitewashing as the chapter's lasting image.

beats.text: That's the formula. [BEAT] It even gets you a plaque.
beats.why: The DOJ building is the institution that issues the fines — the 'plaques' corporations receive for breaking the law. Sardonic callback: the formula earns you formal government recognition, a certificate of acceptable wrongdoing.
beats.sfx_motivation: Sharp single impact on 'formula' — punctuates the thesis callback before the character reckoning begins.

beats.text: Elliana Esquivel is still making art in Charlotte.
beats.why: Elliana Esquivel is a digital artist whose style was scraped without consent. HarperCollins represents the publishing/copyright industry fighting the same AI scraping battle — places her story within the broader creator-rights ecosystem she's navigating.

beats.text: She pivoted to 3D — not because she chose to, but because the alternative was watching her style get reproduced for free.
beats.why: While Esquivel was forced to abandon her 2D style, OpenAI raised $730 billion — built on scraped art including hers. The contrast of one artist's survival pivot against hundreds of billions in AI valuation makes the power asymmetry visceral.

beats.text: [BEAT] If the settlement arrives, her share might cover a month of rent. The model keeps running.
beats.why: The settlement 'might cover a month of rent' — showing a suburban house grounds the inadequacy of the AI scraping payout in concrete financial reality. The aerial shot bridges Esquivel's story to the housing theme that runs through the whole film.

beats.text: Seventy-four percent of Facebook users still don't know the platform profiles them. The data harvested in 2014 was never deleted.
beats.why: 74% of Facebook users don't know they're profiled, and data harvested in 2014 was never deleted — the Facebook HQ building as the institution that is still holding a decade of private data. The permanence of the building mirrors the permanence of the data.

beats.text: [BEAT] The models built on it were refined. Chris Vialpondo is still in Seattle. Still working two jobs.
beats.why: Chris Vialpondo is 'still in Seattle, still working two jobs' — the Queen Anne neighborhood grounds his continued presence in the city where RealPage's algorithm priced him out. Showing Seattle makes his inability to leave feel real, not abstract.

beats.text: [BEAT] The algorithm that raised his rent is still running. His fifty percent increase was not a market decision.
beats.why: The algorithm is still running — this image specifically depicts RealPage's rent coordination antitrust story, making visible the software mechanism behind Vialpondo's 50% increase. His rent wasn't raised by a market; it was raised by a server.

beats.text: It was a formula.
beats.why: The three-word thesis statement 'It was a formula' lands on the NYSE trading floor — the place where human cost is converted into margin. Every case study in this film traces back to a financial optimization decision made by people in rooms like this one.
beats.sfx_motivation: Single hard impact on the thesis line — the climactic three-word reveal earns one sharp hit to let it land.

beats.text: The Grush-Saunby memo put a dollar value on a human life in 1977. [BEAT] Two hundred thousand dollars.
beats.why: The Grush-Saunby memo valued a human life at $200,000 — this crash test still shows the Pinto exploding on impact, making visceral what the memo reduced to a line item. It is the origin point of corporate life valuation, and the image should feel like an accusation.

beats.text: Purdue's settlement valued each opioid death at nine thousand. Facebook's fine valued each compromised user at fifty-seven dollars.
beats.why: The descending ladder: Ford $200K → Purdue $9K per opioid death → Facebook $57 per compromised user. Purdue's headquarters as the institution that settled 600,000+ deaths for $9,000 each. The building stands — the Sacklers kept their billions. The formula worked.

beats.text: The AI settlements value each stolen book at three thousand dollars. [BEAT] Elliana's illustrations? Not priced yet. Your Reddit posts?
beats.why: Bloomberg broadcast graphic showing Meta and Google financial data — the AI companies profiting from scraped content while narration announces the settlement price: $3,000 per stolen book. The broadcast aesthetic frames this as documented public fact, not accusation.

beats.text: Your YouTube comments? Your blog from 2016?
beats.why: Blurry close-up of a smartphone screen — the personal device that holds your comments, blogs, and posts. As narration pivots to 'Your YouTube comments? Your blog from 2016?' this image collapses the distance: your device, your content, their asset.

beats.text: They'll get priced. [BEAT] And if fifty years of history tells you anything — [PAUSE:1.5] you won't like the number.
beats.why: 'Fifty years of history' is a direct invocation of 1977 — Ford priced human lives and chose the cheaper option. Holding on the Pinto through the 1.5s pause lets the viewer complete the arc themselves: from the cost-benefit memo to their Reddit post. No narration needed.

beats.text: The law doesn't prevent corporate crime. [BEAT] It prices it.
beats.why: The ornate coffered ceiling of the DOJ interior — the architecture of justice. Against 'The law doesn't prevent corporate crime. It prices it.' this image is deliberate irony: the beautiful institution housing the machinery of pricing. The thesis text on screen over this image is the visual thesis statement.

beats.sfx_motivation: Single hard impact punctuates the central thesis landing as on-screen text — the payoff of the entire documentary

beats.text: The question was never whether they'd break the law.
beats.why: An older man in a suit gesturing on the NYSE trading floor — the decision-maker archetype. 'The question was never whether they'd break the law' is spoken to this man, in this room, where financial logic has always overridden legal constraint.

beats.text: The question is what you're worth. Sources: NHTSA, Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co.
beats.why: Dark, grainy 1977 archive footage of the Pinto crash — the direct visual answer to 'The question is what you're worth.' Ford already answered this question at $200K per life. The degraded image quality forces the viewer to feel the distance between then and now — and realize the formula hasn't changed.
beats.sfx_motivation: Low drone holds under 'what you're worth' through the final beat — sustains dread into the sources roll
